items.title: Randy Sandke interviewed by Monk Rowe, Aspen, Colorado, October 10, 1997
items.q: Well you’ve certainly played with a long list of the really established veterans, and they seem to embrace your approach. The World’s Greatest Jazz Band and Benny Carter.

ctx.x: Yeah. And I mean that brings up another kind of interesting facet is this whole idea, which I’ve really had to face, of playing older styles which are really basically formed. Like these styles are set, but to try to play it, I mean like here is, okay I have this career, this is what I do. Is it possible to do it in a creative way and in a personal way? And I have come to the belief that yes it is. I don’t mean to hold myself as a great example, but people like Kenny Davern, Warren Vache, Scott Hamilton, to me…

Well you’ve certainly played with a long list of the really established veterans, and they seem to embrace your approach. The World’s Greatest Jazz Band and Benny Carter. Is there a group of people that you really, really look forward to playing with?

Well I feel that like one of the problems that I have is that when I do my own records or these projects which are more modern, that even conceptually I might have an idea of what I want to do but there’s a difference between that and playing every night in a certain context. This is the context I usually find myself in. And again, I love these guys, I love playing the music. But I would also love to play, say, Smitty Smith is doing “The Tonight Show” now but if he weren’t, work with him. I feel like I would grow…
